source.title: Open problems in membrane computing and how not to solve them

accepted.question_text: Can every polynomial-time confluent recogniser P-system family for decision problems be simulated, with at most polynomial overhead, by a deterministic recogniser P-system family of the same sufficiently powerful model, or is there a variant of P systems in which confluent nondeterminism is strictly stronger than determinism? Here confluent means that multiple computations may occur but all computations agree on the final accepting or rejecting result, while deterministic means that the initial configuration has a single computation; the question is especially constrained by send-in communication rules that cannot distinguish among membranes with the same label and electrical charge.

Do polynomial-time uniform and semi-uniform families of sufficiently powerful P systems, such as standard P systems with active membranes, recognize the same decision languages? In the semi-uniform setting, a polynomial-time Turing machine M receives the entire input string x and outputs an encoding of a recogniser P system Pi_x; in the uniform setting, one polynomial-time machine F receives only n = |x| and builds a skeleton Pi_n valid for every input of that length, while another polynomial-time machine E receives x and produces an input multiset w that is placed into Pi_n.

In converting a polynomial-time semi-uniform P-system construction into a uniform one, is the ability of the semi-uniform constructor M to generate super-polynomially many different membrane structures for inputs of the same length ever computationally useful, or can every such use be eliminated while preserving polynomial time and the recognized language? The obstacle is that a uniform machine F, given only input length n, cannot generally build a polynomial-size skeleton containing all possible structures produced by M on length-n inputs.

For P-system variants in which an isolated single membrane working in polynomial time has only P computational power, can the internal behavior of each membrane be replaced by a polynomial-time Turing-machine simulation so that all additional power beyond P comes solely from membrane division, communication, and the resulting network structure? A key subproblem is whether a single charged membrane can feasibly count exponentially many identical objects entering in parallel, effectively converting a unary multiplicity of incoming objects into a binary count.

For polynomial-time cell-like P systems with active membranes, what is the complexity-theoretic power as a function of division depth? In particular, after division depth 0 characterizes P, division depth 1 characterizes P^#P, and polynomial division depth characterizes PSPACE, does increasing any fixed constant division depth d to d + 1 form a proper hierarchy with matching upper bounds, and what class is obtained at intermediate depths such as O(log n)?

For active-membrane P systems, what is the relationship between computational power obtained by allowing non-confluence and computational power obtained by using deep membrane structures? The setting is that shallow membrane structures can still perform exponentially many parallel computations but collect results in the outermost membrane, deep structures combine results hierarchically, and known shallow non-confluent systems can achieve PSPACE power.

trace.notes: Normalized the single input URL as a zbMATH resolver locator for document identifier 7002232. The normalized source name for persistence is zbmath-7002232.

zbMATH REST metadata identified the exact work as title Open problems in membrane computing and how not to solve them, authors Alberto Leporati, Luca Manzoni, Giancarlo Mauri, Antonio E. Porreca, and Claudio Zandron, year 2018, DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-00265-7_15. Metadata was used only to identify and verify the work.

Bounded exact-work recovery searched by exact title and DOI. An author-hosted PDF at https://aeporreca.org/papers/open-problems-in-membrane-computing-how-not-to-solve-them.pdf matched the exact title and authors, returned application/pdf, and was downloaded as the readable primary artifact.

Mapped a 10-page PDF. Section hierarchy: title and abstract; 1 Introduction; 2 Confluence vs determinism; 2.1 Simulation of priorities; 3 Semi-uniformity vs uniformity; 3.1 Building and filling the membrane structure at runtime; 4 Membrane division vs internal evolution; 4.1 Putting a Turing machine inside a membrane; 5 Deep vs shallow membrane structures; References. Key terminology includes recogniser P systems, confluence, determinism, send-in communication rules, semi-uniform and uniform P-system families, membrane division, active membranes, division depth, P, P^#P, and PSPACE. Likely open-problem regions are Sections 2 through 5.

Section 2 asks whether confluent nondeterminism can always be avoided or whether some P-system variant makes it strictly stronger than determinism; Section 2.1 explains why rule priorities do not remove send-in nondeterminism.
Section 3 states the conjecture that polynomial-time uniformity and semi-uniformity coincide for powerful enough P systems after defining both family conditions.

Section 3.1 isolates the obstacle that a semi-uniform construction may generate too many same-length membrane structures for a uniform skeleton to contain polynomially, and asks whether that abundance is actually useful.

Section 4 and Section 4.1 frame the open issue of replacing internal membrane behavior by Turing-machine simulations, with the remaining obstacle that a single charged membrane may need to count exponentially many incoming objects.
Section 5 asks for the complexity power of active-membrane systems as division depth varies, including a conjectured proper hierarchy at constant depths and the uncharacterized O(log n) case.
Section 5 also asks how power from non-confluence relates to power from deep membrane structures after contrasting shallow collection of results with hierarchical combination in deeper structures.
Expanded the source question with the source definitions of confluent recogniser behavior, deterministic behavior, and the send-in communication obstacle.
Expanded the broad conjecture by inlining the source definitions of semi-uniform and uniform P-system families.
Rewrote the two adjacent source questions as one self-contained problem about whether super-polynomially many same-length membrane structures are ever computationally essential.
Combined the Turing-machine-normal-form issue with the explicit counting obstacle because the latter is the unresolved condition needed for the former approach.
Expanded division-depth terminology using the source's stated depth-0, depth-1, polynomial-depth, constant-depth, and O(log n) cases.
Expanded the relation question with the source's contrast between shallow collection, deep hierarchical combination, and shallow non-confluent PSPACE power.

No near-duplicates were merged. The broad uniformity question q_002 and the same-length membrane-structure subproblem q_003 were kept distinct because q_003 is a specific obstruction inside one proposed proof strategy.

All accepted items include self-contained question text, page-located source evidence, solved-status metadata, and no source-pointing language. No item is marked solved because the primary source explicitly presents these as open problems and does not mark any extracted item solved.
